strengths: The idea of using a VLM's Yes/No log-odds as a fully differentiable semantic and spatial critic is clean and well-motivated, and the paper convincingly demonstrates its versatility by plugging the same reward into two very different paradigms (SDS-style optimization and test-time guidance of a native 3D DiT sampler).

Quantitative results on the GPTEval3D benchmark (Table 1) show consistent improvement over all baselines across all six metrics, including strong reward-model baselines like DreamReward and DreamDPO, which supports the central claim for the optimization-based paradigm.

Ablations in Sec. 5.3 are informative: removing the geometric query or switching to single-view input both degrade quality (Janus artifacts, floating parts), directly supporting the dual-query and multi-view design choices.

The limitations section is honest and specific, acknowledging that the reward under-utilizes the VLM's visual reasoning on long prompts and identifying concrete future directions (disentangled semantic/geometry feedback, hierarchical query engineering).
weaknesses: The evaluation of the feed-forward/test-time-guidance paradigm is weak and potentially cherry-picked. Table 2 is computed only 'on all cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4' — a handful of hand-selected failure cases — rather than a broad prompt set or standard benchmark. The sweeping claim that test-time guidance 'actively steers the iterative sampling process of SOTA native 3D models to correct severe spatial errors' is thus not supported by statistically meaningful evidence.

There is a metric inconsistency in Table 2: CLIP-D is marked with a downward arrow (implying lower is better) and VLM3D's 0.19 is bolded as best, yet the text claims 'the substantial gain in CLIP-D demonstrates that our rVLM effectively steers the sampling process towards better text-semantic alignment.' Either the arrow or the interpretation is wrong; this kind of error undermines confidence in the quantitative analysis.

Potential evaluation circularity: the method optimizes toward a VLM's judgment, and the primary benchmark evaluation (GPTEval3D) is itself performed by a VLM judge (GPT-4o-mini). While the judge differs from the reward backbone, VLM-judged metrics plausibly favor outputs shaped by VLM feedback; no human study is provided to confirm the gains transfer to human preference.

Novelty is modest relative to the framing. Backpropagating through VLM/CLIP logits as a differentiable reward is well established in 2D generation and reward-model literature, and prior works already use VLM-style rewards in text-to-3D (e.g., DreamReward/DreamDPO). The 'dual-query' design is essentially two criteria concatenated into a single prompt with a single log-odds signal; no ablation compares this against separate semantic/geometry rewards, which weakens the claim that the dual-query formulation is a core contribution.

Key methodological details needed for reproducibility are missing or deferred: the number of rendered views N, view selection, how the gradient ∇_{z_t} r_VLM in Eq. (10) is obtained through the differentiable rendering of an intermediate DiT latent prediction, memory/compute overhead of backpropagating through a 7B VLM at every sampling step, and the annealing schedule for λ_VLM are all unspecified in the main paper (and no supplementary material is included with the submission).

The test-time guidance is only compared against the unguided baselines (CLAY, Hunyuan3D); there is no comparison with alternative refinement or test-time-guidance strategies for feed-forward 3D models, so the relative merit of the approach within this paradigm is unknown.

Writing and bibliography are sloppy in places: duplicate references ([1]/[3] and [28]/[29], [43]/[44]), a typo ('guidace'), and inconsistent notation, which suggests the manuscript needed another careful revision pass.

The premise that VLMs provide reliable 3D spatial understanding is asserted but not validated in isolation (e.g., how well does the Qwen2.5-VL critic's Yes/No judgment correlate with actual geometric defects?), so gradient noise and reward-hacking behavior of the critic are not characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and current problem: both SDS-based and native 3D feed-forward pipelines suffer from fine-grained semantic and spatial failures, and framing a VLM as a unified differentiable critic is a sensible angle.

Demonstrating the same critic signal in two distinct paradigms (as a reward in SDS optimization and as test-time guidance for a DiT-based 3D diffusion sampler) is a nice unifying demonstration of generality.

Results on the GPTEval3D benchmark (Table 1) show consistent gains over a broad set of established baselines across all six metrics, and the ablations (geometry query, multi-view vs. single-view input, Fig. 6) are relevant and support the dual-query and multi-view design choices.
The limitations section is honest and specific (e.g., the reward formulation still misses fine details on long prompts, and the analysis of why is insightful).
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core technical idea — extracting a differentiable reward from a VLM's 'Yes/No' token logits — is essentially the VQAScore recipe (Lin et al., 2024) transplanted from text-to-image to text-to-3D, but this closely related line of work is not cited or discussed. The 'dual-query' contribution amounts to prompt engineering (two clauses in one prompt), and the claim of being 'the first attempt to establish a principled path' to inject VLM understanding into generative pipelines overstates the novelty.

The feed-forward evaluation (Table 2, Sec. 5.2) is seriously under-powered and potentially cherry-picked: it is computed on 'all cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4', i.e., a tiny hand-selected set of failure-prone prompts, with no standard benchmark, no variance or significance testing. FID/CLIP-FID on a handful of samples is not a meaningful statistic. Comparing VLM-guided Hunyuan3D against CLAY also conflates base-model differences with the guidance effect; the proper ablation (same backbone with/without guidance) is not tabulated.

Metric reporting is inconsistent and confusing: CLIP-D is marked with a down-arrow in Table 2 (text-shape alignment should be higher-is-better, and 0.19 vs 0.22–0.23 as an 'improvement' is suspicious), and the claimed 60 seconds per asset with test-time guidance is hard to reconcile with running a 7B VLM forward and backward at each of 50 sampling steps; no cost/overhead analysis is given.

The GPTEval3D evaluation re-runs baselines with GPT-4o-mini rather than the original GPT-4V judge, and using a VLM-family model as the evaluator risks evaluator bias in favor of a method whose reward is itself a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL); this circularity is not discussed.

Key methodological details are vague or deferred: Eq. 10's 'conceptual' update leaves unspecified how the 3D latent at an intermediate denoising step is decoded/differentiably rendered, how gradients flow through the decoder, the number/resolution of views, and the concrete λ annealing schedule — all material to reproduction.

Presentation issues: duplicated and inconsistent references ([1]/[2]/[3] are the same technical report; GPTEval3D appears as both [43] and [44]), typos ('guidace', 'VM3D'), and Fig. 2's rendered query text contains formatting artifacts, suggesting insufficient polish.
For the optimization-based experiments, all comparisons rely on GPT-judge Elo scores; no human study or independent geometric evaluation is provided to corroborate the perceptual claims.

strengths: The idea of using a large VLM's Yes/No log-odds as a differentiable semantic and spatial critic is simple, clean, and plausibly general, and the paper demonstrates it in two distinct 3D generation paradigms (SDS-style optimization and test-time guidance of a native 3D DiT), which supports the 'general critic' framing.

Quantitative results on GPTEval3D (Table 1) show VLM3D beating a broad set of representative SDS-based baselines (DreamFusion, ProlificDreamer, DreamReward, DreamDPO) on all six metrics, which is a substantial empirical showing if reproducible.

The paper includes targeted ablations (geometry query in the prompt, multi-view vs. single-view VLM input) that directly support the two key design claims, and honest qualitative sensitivity analyses (prompt perturbations, spatial prepositions 'in' vs. 'beside').

The limitations section is candid: the authors show a case (the 'Embracing Peace' statue) where VLM3D improves over the baseline but still misses fine details, and they correctly diagnose that the binary reward underuses the VLM's reasoning ability.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and an important missing related-work thread: the core signal — probability of 'Yes' to a yes/no question about an image (or image set) used as a differentiable reward — is essentially VQAScore-style evaluation (Lin et al., 2024) repurposed for 3D, and VLM-reward guidance for generation has precedents (DreamReward, RLHF-tuned rewards). The claim of being the 'first attempt to establish a principled path to inject VLM understanding into 3D pipelines' is overstated, and VQAScore and closely related VLM-as-reward works are not discussed or compared.

Table 2 appears erroneous or at best confusingly presented: CLIP-D is marked with a down-arrow (lower is better) and VLM3D's *lower* CLIP-D (0.19 vs. 0.23–0.22) is presented as an improvement, contradicting the standard interpretation of CLIP text-shape alignment (higher is better) and the text's own claim of 'substantial gain in CLIP-D'. Either the arrow or the conclusion is wrong, which undermines confidence in the feed-forward experiments.

The feed-forward evaluation is very weak statistically: metrics are computed on 'all cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4' — a handful of cherry-picked prompts — yet the paper claims 'significant improvements across the board'. FID/CLIP-FID on such a tiny sample is not meaningful, no confidence intervals or significance tests are given anywhere, and no human study is provided despite the qualitative nature of the central claims.

Potential judge/reward circularity is not addressed: the method optimizes a VLM-based reward, and the main quantitative benchmark uses a GPT-4o-mini multimodal judge. Multimodal judges are known to share biases with VLMs (e.g., preferring outputs that match VLM-recognizable semantics), so the headline Table 1 gains may partly reflect reward-hacking or judge agreement rather than genuinely better 3D assets.

The test-time guidance method (Sec. 4.3.2) is under-specified: Eq. 10 requires ∇_{z_t} r_VLM, i.e., differentiating from a 3D latent z_t through the DiT's current prediction, the decoder, and a differentiable rendering into multi-view images at every one of 50 sampling steps. The exact pipeline (which decoder, what rendering, gradient checkpointing, memory cost) is relegated to the supplementary material; the claimed 60 s/asset on one A100 with a 7B VLM queried at each step is not clearly justified.

The dual-query 'contribution' is essentially prompt engineering: the two criteria are combined into a single yes/no question, so the two objectives cannot be weighted, attributed, or controlled independently — the authors themselves note this in limitations. No comparison to alternative reward formulations (separate queries, graded scores, pairwise preferences) is provided, and the ablations are purely qualitative.

Presentation and scholarly care issues: duplicated references ([1]/[2]/[3], [28]/[29], [43]/[44]), typos ('guidace', 'VM3D'), and Fig. 4/6 layout confusion; the ablation in Fig. 6 mentions a 'bicycle that leaves a trail of flowers' prompt whose geometry-relevance is unclear.

Reproducibility concerns: the λ_VLM annealing schedule is described only qualitatively, the geometric score in Table 2 is undefined ('a comprehensive Geometry score'), and key implementation details are deferred to supplementary material that is not part of the submission as reviewed.

strengths: The core idea—backpropagating the 'Yes/No' log-odds of a VLM as a differentiable semantic-and-spatial critic—is simple, principled, and genuinely useful, and the paper demonstrates it consistently across two very different 3D generation paradigms (SDS-style optimization and test-time guidance of a native 3D DiT like Hunyuan3D), which supports the generality claim.

Quantitative evaluation on GPTEval3D (110 prompts) shows VLM3D beating all baselines including DreamReward and DreamDPO on every metric, and the feed-forward guidance improves CLIP-D, FID, CLIP-FID, and the geometry metric over both Hunyuan3D and CLAY (Table 2).

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough: geometric-query ablation, multi-view vs. single-view input, guidance scheduling (Table 5), prompt design variants (Tables 4, Fig. 6-7), VLM-only vs. SDS-only (Table 7), and external 3D-native metrics (ULIP/Uni3D, Table 6), which go beyond cherry-picked qualitative results.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-2), hyperparameters, annealing schedules, baseline configurations, computational overhead profiling (Table 3), and an attached code package with a promised public release.

The engineering contribution of making the VLM pathway fully differentiable (re-engineering image preprocessors that detach gradients) is a real, non-obvious practical contribution that others will benefit from, and it is documented in the supplementary.
The limitations section is honest and specific, acknowledging that the reward formulation under-leverages the VLM's own reasoning on fine-grained details (e.g., the 'Embracing Peace' statue).
weaknesses: Originality is incremental. Using VQA/VLM log-likelihood as a reward or guidance signal is closely related to prior work (e.g., VQAScore-style binary-yes evaluation and its use as a reward, DreamReward/DreamDPO reward optimization for 3D, and reward backpropagation through pretrained scorers). The claim of being 'the first attempt to establish a principled and generalizable path' is overstated; the main novelty reduces to applying VLM log-odds rewards to 3D generation plus prompt engineering of a dual-criteria query.

The 'dual-query' contribution is largely prompt engineering: a single yes/no prompt that combines content and geometric criteria. Ablations show it helps, but there is no disentangled control (e.g., separate weighted rewards) and no analysis of gradient conflicts between the two criteria beyond gradient-norm reporting in Table 4.

The feed-forward evaluation is small (only 24 prompts) and uses a self-defined 'Geometry Score' (Chamfer/Hausdorff/P2M averaged) whose reference and protocol are under-specified in the main text; Table 2 also contains apparent labeling inconsistencies (e.g., CLIP-D marked with a down arrow, unusual FID magnitudes of 274-338), which undermines confidence in the quantitative claims for that paradigm.

Potential evaluator bias: the headline optimization results rely on GPT-4o-mini pairwise Elo, and the method is specifically optimized against a VLM critic, so VLM-guided outputs may be systematically favored by LLM/VLM judges; no human evaluation is reported to corroborate the preferences.

Dependence on a single VLM backbone (Qwen2.5-VL 7B) is weakly justified; alternatives (PaliGemma, IDEFICS) were tried but only 'preliminary analysis' is mentioned with no numbers, so robustness of the critic signal across VLMs is unverified.

Cost and reward-hacking risks are underexplored: VLM-guided optimization needs 49 GB and 2.2 h per asset, and the paper does not analyze failure modes of optimizing against a VLM's yes/no log-odds (e.g., exploiting VLM biases, texture tricks that fool the VLM but not humans), beyond one qualitative limitation example.

Presentation issues: repeated/malformed citation keys (Bai et al. 2025a/b), typos ('guidace', 'VM3D'), a missing URL after 'Code is available at' in the abstract, and duplicated reference entries reduce polish.

strengths: The core idea of using a VLM's Yes/No log-odds as a differentiable critic is simple, general, and plausibly useful across two distinct 3D generation paradigms (SDS-based optimization and test-time guidance of native 3D diffusion models like Hunyuan3D).

The paper correctly identifies a real and timely failure mode of SOTA feed-forward 3D models (part assembly, spatial incoherence) and shows qualitative examples where guidance substantially improves them (Figs. 1, 4, 10, 11).

The engineering of an end-to-end differentiable pathway through the VLM (re-engineering image preprocessors that detach gradients) is a genuine, nontrivial practical contribution, and pseudo-code plus hyperparameter details in the appendix support reproducibility.
The optimization-based results on the GPTEval3D benchmark (Table 1) show consistent gains over reasonable SDS-based baselines (DreamReward, DreamDPO, MVDream) across all six metrics.
The limitations section is candid and informative (e.g., failure to capture fine details in the 'Embracing Peace' example, observation that the reward under-uses the VLM's reasoning).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: scoring with VLM Yes/No token logits is essentially a VQAScore-style reward, and gradient-based VLM reward optimization for generative models is well established (AlignProp, DreamReward, DPO-style text-to-3D methods). The 'dual-query critic' is in fact a single prompt with two criteria collapsed into one Yes/No logit, so the framing overstates a fairly minor prompt-engineering choice.

The feed-forward evaluation (Table 2) is weak: only 24 prompts, drawn from cases shown in Figs. 1 and 4 where baselines visibly fail (a selected, adversarial set), and FID/CLIP-FID on ~24 assets is statistically meaningless. The comparison is also not apples-to-apples: VLM3D uses MVDream to generate a reference image and then runs image-to-3D with guidance, while baselines run text-to-3D directly.

Metric definitions and reporting are confusing or likely erroneous: Table 2 labels CLIP-D with a downward arrow where higher alignment should be better (and lower value 0.19 is reported as best); the 'Geometry Score' is only defined in the appendix. CLAY is evaluated via an online demo rather than controlled conditions.

Ablations are largely circular: the prompt-design (Table 4) and guidance-scheduling (Table 5) ablations are evaluated by the VLM reward itself (and CLIP similarity, a 2D metric), not by the benchmark quality metrics used for headline claims, so they do not validate end quality.

Potential reward hacking / over-optimization of the VLM judge is not analyzed, even though the main benchmark (GPTEval3D) uses GPT-4o-mini as an evaluator and the method optimizes a VLM-derived reward; a bias discussion or human study is needed.

The test-time guidance formulation (Eq. 10) is given only 'conceptually'; the exact interaction with the velocity prediction, CFG, and the feed-forward sampler is under-specified relative to Algorithm 2, and the number of views N and viewpoint sampling scheme are never stated.

Some claims are not supported: 'significantly outperforms' and 'proves that our rVLM can serve as an effective spatial critic' rest on small, non-selected-free evaluations; several baseline results are copied from other papers rather than run under matched conditions.

Presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('guidace', 'VM3D'), a truncated code URL ('Code is available at'), a duplicated Qwen2.5-VL citation (2025a/2025b), and the impact statement is boilerplate with no discussion of risks specific to generated 3D content.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: both optimization-based (SDS) and native 3D feed-forward pipelines suffer from coarse semantic alignment and spatial/part-assembly failures, and the proposed VLM-based critic is a sensible mechanism to attack both failure modes.

The core idea is demonstrated convincingly across two very different generation paradigms (SDS-based optimization and test-time guidance of Hunyuan3D), which supports the claimed generality of the critic signal rather than a single-pipeline trick.

The technical realization is non-trivial: the authors identify and fix the gradient detachment in VLM image preprocessors (re-engineering them to be fully torch-tensor based), enabling end-to-end backpropagation of the Yes/No log-odds reward — a practical contribution others can reuse.

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough: dual-query vs. content-only vs. geometry-only prompts, multi-view vs. single-view inputs, guidance scheduling (Table 5), VLM-only vs. SDS-only vs. combined (Table 7), VLM backbone selection, and 3D-native metrics (ULIP/Uni3D, Table 6) go beyond the minimum.

The paper is generally well written and honest about limitations (e.g., failure to capture fine details in long prompts on the 'Embracing Peace' example), and code is promised/attached, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest and the related-work positioning overstates firstness. Using VLM/reward log-likelihoods (Yes/No log-odds) as differentiable alignment signals has clear precedent: DreamReward and DreamDPO for 3D, and VQAScore-style Yes/No log-probability rewards for text-to-image guidance. The core method (Eq. 8) is a scalar logit difference plus prompt engineering; the 'dual-query' is a single prompt with two bullet criteria. The claim of being 'the first attempt to establish a principled and generalizable path' is not adequately supported.

The feed-forward evaluation (Table 2) is weak: it is based on only 24 prompts that are explicitly the cases shown in Fig. 1 and 4, i.e., prompts where the baseline is already known to fail. This introduces a clear selection bias in favor of the proposed method, and there is no comparison against any other test-time guidance or refinement baseline in this setting.

Table 2 has metric-direction inconsistencies: CLIP-D and FID are marked with down-arrows (↓) while the text reports 'gains' in CLIP-D and lower is better for FID/CLIP-FID but the numbers reported for the proposed method are lowest — the sign conventions and reporting need clarification, and 'Geometry' is a self-defined metric without a reference description in the main text.

The feed-forward pipeline is image-conditioned (an MVDream reference image is generated first, then Hunyuan3D is guided). This introduces a confound: part of the semantic improvement may come from the stronger image condition rather than the VLM critic, and no ablation isolates this.

Evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini as judge for the main benchmark, which introduces LLM-judge bias; there is no human study to validate the ranking, and the VLM reward backbone (Qwen2.5-VL) is related in spirit to the judge despite being a different model family.

Quantitative evidence that the test-time guidance fixes 'severe spatial errors' is largely qualitative (Figs. 1, 4, 10, 11); the deterministic Geometry score is computed on the small, biased 24-prompt set rather than a broader, unbiased prompt set.

Presentation and reference hygiene issues: duplicated references (Wu et al. 2024a/2024b are the same paper; Bai et al. 2025a/2025b duplicates), typos ('guidace', 'VM3D'), and a Figure 4 with confusing duplicated panel labels. Minor, but they detract from polish.

The cost is non-trivial and should be weighed against the benefit: 49 GB memory and 2.2 h per asset for the optimization pipeline, and 2× runtime (60s extra per asset, 53 GB) for the feed-forward pipeline; a stronger discussion of the cost/benefit trade-off relative to simpler alternatives is missing.
